content:
Neck arthritis, often called cervical spondylosis, is age-related wear in the joints and discs of the neck. It is very common after 40 and often causes no symptoms. When it does, it usually causes neck pain and stiffness that comes and goes. Most people improve with regular movement, good posture and simple pain relief. Rarely it presses on nerves, which needs medical assessment.

Symptoms

  • neck pain and stiffness, often worse after staying in one position
  • pain spreading to the shoulders or base of the skull
  • headaches starting at the back of the head
  • grinding or clicking when turning the head
  • reduced movement, such as difficulty looking over your shoulder when driving

Symptoms usually flare and settle over weeks.

When nerves are involved

Bony changes can sometimes narrow the space for nerves:

  • trapped nerve (radiculopathy): pain, pins and needles, numbness or weakness down one arm into the hand
  • pressure on the spinal cord (myelopathy): less common but more serious. Signs include clumsy hands, difficulty with buttons or writing, unsteady walking and changes in bladder control. This needs prompt assessment.

Other types of arthritis in the neck

Rheumatoid arthritis can affect the top of the neck. If you have RA and develop new neck pain, especially with tingling in the arms, tell your rheumatology team. Ankylosing spondylitis can also cause neck stiffness.

Self-care that helps

  • keep moving. Gentle neck exercises several times a day are better than keeping it still.
  • simple pain relief. Ask your pharmacist about painkillers or anti-inflammatory gels that suit you.
  • heat from a wheat bag or warm shower can ease stiffness
  • check your posture, particularly at a desk or on your phone. Bring screens up to eye level.
  • sleep with a supportive pillow that keeps your neck in line with your spine. Avoid using too many pillows.
  • take regular breaks from driving, screens and close work

Neck collars are not usually recommended, as they can make the neck stiffer.

Gentle neck exercises

Do these slowly, within a comfortable range:

  • chin tucks: sitting tall, gently draw your chin back to make a double chin, hold, then relax
  • side bends: tilt your ear towards your shoulder, hold, then repeat on the other side
  • rotations: turn your head slowly to look over each shoulder
  • shoulder rolls: roll your shoulders backwards in circles

Repeat each a few times, several times a day. Stop if an exercise causes pins and needles or pain into the arm.

NHS treatment

If symptoms do not improve after a few weeks, see your GP or self-refer to physiotherapy if available in your area. A physiotherapist can give you a tailored exercise programme and advice on posture and activities. For persistent nerve symptoms, you may be referred for an MRI scan or to a specialist. Surgery is only considered for a small number of people with significant nerve or spinal cord pressure.

Work and daily life

  • set up your workstation with your screen at eye level and your keyboard close
  • use a headset for long phone calls
  • in the car, adjust the head restraint and mirrors, and turn your body to check blind spots if needed
  • spread jobs such as painting ceilings or hanging washing across the day

Outlook

Most people with neck arthritis keep active and manage well. Pain often comes and goes over the years, and flares usually settle within a few weeks. Staying active and keeping your neck moving is the best long-term approach.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • neck pain with new weakness, clumsiness or numbness in both arms or legs, problems walking, or problems controlling your bladder or bowels
  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
